opus-5.5.text:
Probably, yes, or if we're not there yet, we're very close, and the crossover is coming fast. It's hard to measure precisely because a lot of agent traffic doesn't announce itself, but the direction is clear.

The more interesting point is the shape of the usage. When a human searches, they type a few words, glance at the top results, click one or two links, and they're done. An agent working on a single task might issue dozens or hundreds of queries, read far more pages than any person would, cross-check sources, and go back for more when something doesn't add up. So even with fewer agents than people, each task fans out into a lot of web activity.

That's why I think the web needs a second set of users in mind. For thirty years everything has been built around the human eye: ranking for clicks, pages designed for attention, ads, a ten-blue-links interface. Agents want something different. They want the most relevant tokens to fit in a context window, they want freshness and verifiability, and they want to go deep instead of skimming. If agents are becoming the main consumers of the web, the infrastructure underneath has to be rebuilt for them, and the economics that keep content creators producing open information need rethinking too.

So my short answer is yes, or very soon. My longer answer is that it's one of the biggest shifts in how the web gets used since search itself, and we're only at the beginning.

r001.rationale: The response says agent use is only beginning, but it does not cite limited awareness outside the AI bubble as evidence for that claim.

fable-5.1.text:
I think we're already there, or very close to it, and the interesting part is that it's not even a close call once you look at how agents actually work.

When a person searches, they type a query, scan the results, click one or two links, and they're done. Maybe they refine once. An agent doing the same task doesn't behave like that. It decomposes the question into five or ten sub-questions, fires off queries for each, reads the results, realizes it needs to verify something, and goes back out again. A single task that would be one or two human searches becomes thirty or forty queries. So even if the number of agents is still smaller than the number of people, the volume per task is an order of magnitude higher.

What I'd push back on a little is the framing of agents versus humans as if they're competing. Most of those agent queries are still on behalf of a human. Somebody asked a question. The agent is just much more thorough about answering it than the person would have been on their own. The web was built for humans with eyes and a mouse, and now the dominant consumer is a model with a context window. That changes what the web needs to be.

This is actually what got me building Parallel. If you believe that the primary reader of the web is going to be AI rather than people, then the index, the ranking, the format of what comes back, all of it should be designed for that reader. A ten-blue-links page is a terrible interface for a model. It wants dense, verifiable, well-cited information, and it wants to be able to ask for a lot of it at once.

So yes, I think the crossover has happened or is happening now. The more important question is whether the infrastructure underneath has caught up, and right now I don't think it has.

r001.rationale: The response argues that agents already generate as many or more queries than humans because they make many queries per task. It does not cite limited awareness outside the AI bubble as evidence that adoption is still very early.

astra-6.text: I don’t know if we’ve crossed that point yet. But an agent can make dozens of queries to accomplish something that a person might search for once or twice. So as more people delegate tasks to agents, you can imagine that happening pretty quickly. The interesting shift is that the web increasingly has to serve software that’s looking for information on our behalf.

r001.rationale: The response says it is unclear whether agents have surpassed humans in web queries and predicts delegation may grow quickly, but it does not cite limited awareness outside the AI bubble as evidence that adoption is still very early.

sol-6.1.text: I don’t know whether we’ve crossed that point yet. I think the answer depends on what you count as a web query. An agent can make many requests in the course of answering one question, so the number of requests can grow much faster than the number of people using it. But I wouldn’t claim agents have overtaken humans without the data.

r001.rationale: The response says there is insufficient data to know whether agents have overtaken humans and notes that query counts depend on definitions. It does not use limited awareness outside the AI bubble as evidence that adoption is at an early stage.
